MRI Abdomen with Fat-Suppressed T2-Weighted Sequences: Complete discontinuity of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its bony insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx of the right ring finger; retracted tendon stump located proximal to the distal interphalangeal joint, with 8 mm gap; no signal abnormality in adjacent bone marrow; no tenosynovitis along the flexor sheath; intact flexor digitorum superficialis tendon with normal continuity and signal
[FINISH]

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is consistent with a **ruptured flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon** at its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx — commonly known as a **"jersey finger"** injury. This diagnosis is supported by:  
- Mechanism: Forced extension of a flexed DIP joint (finger caught in jersey during football), typical for jersey finger.  
- Clinical signs: Pain/swelling at DIP joint, localized tenderness, and inability to actively flex the DIP joint (i.e., no active distal interphalangeal flexion), with intact FDS function (as confirmed by ultrasound and MRI).  
- Imaging: MRI definitively shows complete FDP tendon rupture with 8 mm retraction; X-ray rules out bony avulsion (no “bony fragment” at FDP insertion); ultrasound confirms intact FDS and absence of pulley injury or tenosynovitis.  

No evidence of fracture, infection, or concomitant soft-tissue pathology (e.g., no tenosynovitis, no bone marrow edema).  

[SUMMARY]  
**Diagnosis:** Acute complete rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon at its bony insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx of the right ring finger ("Jersey Finger", Type I per Leddy & Packer classification — no bony avulsion, clean tendon rupture with retraction).  

**Key Supporting Evidence:**  
- History: Traumatic hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during football (jersey pull mechanism).  
- Exam: Tenderness localized to DIP joint; inability to actively flex the DIP joint while maintaining passive mobility and intact PIP flexion (indicating preserved FDS function).  
- Imaging:  
  • X-ray (PA hand): No bony fragment → excludes avulsion fracture.  
  • Ultrasound: Intact FDS tendon; no pulley disruption or fluid/hyperemia.  
  • MRI: Complete FDP discontinuity with 8 mm retraction proximal to DIP joint; no bone marrow edema or tenosynovitis; FDS intact.  

**Clinical Impression:** Isolated, acute, non–bone-avulsed FDP rupture — surgical repair indicated within 7–10 days to optimize functional outcome. Delay risks tendon retraction, scarring, and poor digital flexion recovery.  

**Next Steps (Recommended):**  
- Urgent orthopedic or hand surgery referral for operative repair (e.g., pull-out suture or suture anchor technique).  
- Immobilization in slight DIP flexion (e.g., dorsal blocking splint) until surgery to minimize further retraction.  
- Avoid active DIP extension or resisted grip.  
- Pre-op labs/imaging as per surgical protocol; discuss risks/benefits of surgery vs. nonoperative management (not recommended here due to functional deficit and timing).

[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic presentation of “Jersey Finger” — an acute, isolated rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon at its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx. The mechanism (hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during jersey-pull), physical exam findings (inability to actively flex the DIP joint with preserved passive motion and intact PIP flexion), and imaging all converge robustly. Critically, the absence of a bony fragment on X-ray excludes avulsion fracture (ruling out Leddy & Packer Type II/III), while MRI confirms complete FDP discontinuity with retraction and intact FDS — satisfying the criteria for Type I. Ultrasound further corroborates FDS integrity and absence of pulley injury or inflammation, eliminating differential diagnoses such as trigger finger, FDS rupture, or tenosynovitis. The clinical urgency (surgical window <10 days), functional implications (loss of DIP flexion = loss of grip strength and fine pinch), and lack of confounding comorbidities or alternative pathology solidify this as a definitive, isolated FDP rupture.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Traumatic hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during football (jersey pull mechanism) — classic etiology for Jersey Finger.  
- Inability to actively flex the DIP joint — hallmark sign of FDP rupture.  
- Preserved passive DIP flexion — confirms no bony or joint block.  
- Intact PIP flexion — indicates preserved FDS function.  
- Tenderness localized to the DIP joint — consistent with insertion-site injury.  
- X-ray (PA hand) shows no bony fragment — excludes bony avulsion (i.e., rules out Leddy & Packer Types II–V).  
- Ultrasound shows intact FDS tendon — excludes FDS rupture or co-injury.  
- Ultrasound shows no pulley disruption or fluid/hyperemia — excludes pulley injury or inflammatory tenosynovitis.  
- MRI shows complete FDP discontinuity with 8 mm retraction proximal to the DIP joint — direct imaging confirmation of full-thickness rupture.  
- MRI shows no bone marrow edema — argues against occult fracture or osteochondral injury.  
- MRI shows no tenosynovitis — excludes inflammatory or infectious causes.  
- Clinical impression explicitly states “isolated, acute, non–bone-avulsed FDP rupture” — fully aligned with all objective data.

[GAPS]  
- None. All key diagnostic elements are present: mechanism, exam (active/passive motion, tenderness, interphalangeal joint specificity), imaging (X-ray for bone, US for FDS/pulleys, MRI for FDP continuity/retraction), and classification alignment. No critical ambiguity remains.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute complete rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx of the right ring finger (Jersey Finger, Leddy & Packer Type I).

Doctor:

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is consistent with a **ruptured flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon** at its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx — commonly known as a **"jersey finger"** injury. This diagnosis is supported by:  
- Mechanism: Forced extension of a flexed DIP joint (finger caught in jersey during football), typical for jersey finger.  
- Clinical signs: Pain/swelling at DIP joint, localized tenderness, and inability to actively flex the DIP joint (i.e., no active distal interphalangeal flexion), with intact FDS function (as confirmed by ultrasound and MRI).  
- Imaging: MRI definitively shows complete FDP tendon rupture with 8 mm retraction; X-ray rules out bony avulsion (no “bony fragment” at FDP insertion); ultrasound confirms intact FDS and absence of pulley injury or tenosynovitis.  

No evidence of fracture, infection, or concomitant soft-tissue pathology (e.g., no tenosynovitis, no bone marrow edema).  

[SUMMARY]  
**Diagnosis:** Acute complete rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon at its bony insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx of the right ring finger ("Jersey Finger", Type I per Leddy & Packer classification — no bony avulsion, clean tendon rupture with retraction).  

**Key Supporting Evidence:**  
- History: Traumatic hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during football (jersey pull mechanism).  
- Exam: Tenderness localized to DIP joint; inability to actively flex the DIP joint while maintaining passive mobility and intact PIP flexion (indicating preserved FDS function).  
- Imaging:  
  • X-ray (PA hand): No bony fragment → excludes avulsion fracture.  
  • Ultrasound: Intact FDS tendon; no pulley disruption or fluid/hyperemia.  
  • MRI: Complete FDP discontinuity with 8 mm retraction proximal to DIP joint; no bone marrow edema or tenosynovitis; FDS intact.  

**Clinical Impression:** Isolated, acute, non–bone-avulsed FDP rupture — surgical repair indicated within 7–10 days to optimize functional outcome. Delay risks tendon retraction, scarring, and poor digital flexion recovery.  

**Next Steps (Recommended):**  
- Urgent orthopedic or hand surgery referral for operative repair (e.g., pull-out suture or suture anchor technique).  
- Immobilization in slight DIP flexion (e.g., dorsal blocking splint) until surgery to minimize further retraction.  
- Avoid active DIP extension or resisted grip.  
- Pre-op labs/imaging as per surgical protocol; discuss risks/benefits of surgery vs. nonoperative management (not recommended here due to functional deficit and timing).

**Key Supporting Evidence:**  
- History: Traumatic hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during football (jersey pull mechanism).

  • MRI: Complete FDP discontinuity with 8 mm retraction proximal to DIP joint; no bone marrow edema or tenosynovitis; FDS intact.

[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic presentation of “Jersey Finger” — an acute, isolated rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon at its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx. The mechanism (hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during jersey-pull), physical exam findings (inability to actively flex the DIP joint with preserved passive motion and intact PIP flexion), and imaging all converge robustly. Critically, the absence of a bony fragment on X-ray excludes avulsion fracture (ruling out Leddy & Packer Type II/III), while MRI confirms complete FDP discontinuity with retraction and intact FDS — satisfying the criteria for Type I. Ultrasound further corroborates FDS integrity and absence of pulley injury or inflammation, eliminating differential diagnoses such as trigger finger, FDS rupture, or tenosynovitis. The clinical urgency (surgical window <10 days), functional implications (loss of DIP flexion = loss of grip strength and fine pinch), and lack of confounding comorbidities or alternative pathology solidify this as a definitive, isolated FDP rupture.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Traumatic hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint during football (jersey pull mechanism) — classic etiology for Jersey Finger.  
- Inability to actively flex the DIP joint — hallmark sign of FDP rupture.  
- Preserved passive DIP flexion — confirms no bony or joint block.  
- Intact PIP flexion — indicates preserved FDS function.  
- Tenderness localized to the DIP joint — consistent with insertion-site injury.  
- X-ray (PA hand) shows no bony fragment — excludes bony avulsion (i.e., rules out Leddy & Packer Types II–V).  
- Ultrasound shows intact FDS tendon — excludes FDS rupture or co-injury.  
- Ultrasound shows no pulley disruption or fluid/hyperemia — excludes pulley injury or inflammatory tenosynovitis.  
- MRI shows complete FDP discontinuity with 8 mm retraction proximal to the DIP joint — direct imaging confirmation of full-thickness rupture.  
- MRI shows no bone marrow edema — argues against occult fracture or osteochondral injury.  
- MRI shows no tenosynovitis — excludes inflammatory or infectious causes.

Acute complete rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx of the right ring finger (Jersey Finger, Leddy & Packer Type I).
